Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan wrote to me at midnight, and said that we must talk; and I knew at once what such a message could mean.

We met the next day at a coffee-house in the town, where he was already before me, bending over his little instrument and looking, I thought, exceedingly nervous; and in a very few minutes he told me that he was not ready for any thing serious, and that it was not me, but himself—that hated and detested phrase.

I wanted to cry, but did not; I only nodded, and said that it was very well, and walked home in the rain, and ate a whole pint of ice-cream.

My companion in the house thought I was carrying my grief too far; and perhaps I was, for I could not tell; but it hurt me still.

rows.text: Ryan wrote to me at midnight, and said that we must talk; and I knew at once what such a message could mean.

We met the next day at a coffee-house in the town, where he was already before me, bending over his little instrument and looking, I thought, exceedingly nervous; and in a very few minutes he told me that he was not ready for any thing serious, and that it was not me, but himself—that hated and detested phrase.

notes.after: in a very few minutes he told me that he was not ready for any thing serious, and that it was not me, but himself

notes.text: The voice's dry naming of the old excuse, which the writer's facts ("it wasn't me, it was him") invite; it is a verdict, not a new incident.
notes.after: that hated and detested phrase

rows.text: I wanted to cry, but did not; I only nodded, and said that it was very well, and walked home in the rain, and ate a whole pint of ice-cream.

notes.after: I wanted to cry, but did not; I only nodded, and said that it was very well

rows.text: My companion in the house thought I was carrying my grief too far; and perhaps I was, for I could not tell; but it hurt me still.

lessons: The chief difference is that your passage names each fact in a bare short sentence, while the author joins the matter into periods and lets the narrator judge it. I turned the message and its meaning into one sentence, and his dismissal into one ("he told me that he was not ready for any thing serious, and that it was not me, but himself"), so the excuse lands with a dry deflating clause. Practise holding two or three facts in one balanced period, and letting feeling show by conduct, as in "I wanted to cry, but did not," rather than by being named outright.

outline.gist: Ryan sends word at midnight; they must talk; she knows what it means
next day they meet at a coffee shop downtown; he is there first, absorbed in a device, looks nervous
he tells her he is not ready for something serious; not her, him
she wants to cry but does not; nods and assents; walk home in rain, eat ice cream
her companion thinks she overreacts; perhaps; but it still hurts

plan.gist: the message at midnight and what it at once betokened
plan.why: The voice opens with the event and its meaning together, so the reader knows the matter from the first sentence.

plan.gist: the next day's meeting and his present state, nervous and absorbed
plan.why: Setting before scene; his manner precedes his words, so the speech that follows is already understood.

plan.gist: his declaration in reported speech, and then its second clause
plan.why: The occasion's two parts in one period; the old excuse lands lightly but fully.

plan.gist: her composure, her assent, the walk in the rain and the ice cream
plan.why: Feeling shown by conduct; grief held in, then given to small comforts.

plan.gist: her companion's judgement, her own allowance, and that it still hurt
plan.why: A turn, a concession, and a short closing sentence that leaves the hurt standing.

faults.quote: that hated and detested phrase
faults.why: This adds a feeling the writer never stated. The writer says only that he said it. The narrator now actively hates the phrase, which is an invented emotional stance, not commentary on what is there.

faults.quote: bending over his little instrument
faults.why: The writer's 'scrolling on his phone' becomes an odd euphemism. It also adds a faintly contemptuous 'little' that the writer did not feel.

faults.quote: in a very few minutes he told me
faults.why: The writer gives no timing. This adds an incident detail, and it blurs the sequence of his being nervous and then speaking.

faults.quote: said that it was very well
faults.why: The writer said 'okay', which is a flat assent. 'Very well' is acceptable, but it shifts the tone slightly toward a formal acquiescence.

faults.quote: carrying my grief too far
faults.why: The roommate thought she was 'overreacting'. This is close but turns the judgement into one about grief and loses the sense of a reaction to the event.

faults.quote: I knew at once what such a message could mean.
faults.why: The rewrite is in first person with modern incident details (coffee-house, ice-cream, text as 'wrote'). The Austen narrator is third-person and ironic, so this reads as period costume over a modern confession. The irony and the wit are thin.

faults.quote: My companion in the house
faults.why: This is a stilted periphrasis for 'roommate'. It is neither Austen's usage nor clear, and 'companion' implies a paid or genteel companion.

faults.quote: and said that it was very well, and walked home in the rain, and ate a whole pint of ice-cream
faults.why: A string of polysyndetic 'and's with 'a whole pint of ice-cream' is bathetic. The anachronism is unmediated and reads as unintended comedy.

faults.quote: in the town
faults.why: The writer's 'downtown' becomes 'in the town', which is vague and drops the sense of a city centre.

faults.quote: cites Northanger Abbey, ch. 6, ¶ 36
faults.why: This is a precise-looking citation for a generic reported-speech move. It is unlikely to be verifiable, and the note does not say what the move is.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The voice's dry naming of the old excuse
faults.why: The note calls 'hated and detested phrase' a verdict, not a new incident. In fact it adds a feeling to the narrator. The note understates the change.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraphs 1 and 4 carry real changes (the 'companion' periphrasis, the concession, the semicolon structure) and receive no notes, so the notes are thin.

faults.quote: But it still hurt.
faults.why: The writer's short closing sentence is folded into a semicolon chain, 'but it hurt me still'. The built outline says the voice leaves the hurt standing in a short sentence. The rewrite did not do this, so the structure notes contradict the result.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the order and facts and gets some period rhythm, but it adds a feeling ('hated and detested'), uses awkward periphrases ('little instrument', 'companion in the house'), and falls into bathos. The notes are sparse and slightly inaccurate, and the lesson is useful but modest.

yours:
A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family took the house next door a week since, with a large cart at the door and two young children about it. The father, without doubt, was an agreeable man; the woman with him rather reserved than affable, being, as we soon learnt, his sister, come to keep him in order and the children in their place.

My mother lost no time in carrying them biscuits, for she was resolved to learn everything of the family; and what she wished to know was not a little; where they came from, what they did for a living, and whether they went to church.

It was soon found that the father was a lawyer, and that he was single — parted, that is, from his wife; and it was on this intelligence that my mother got a look which I knew exactly how to read. She has been trying to settle me for years, as is natural to a mother whose daughter is not yet settled.

rows.text: A new family took the house next door a week since, with a large cart at the door and two young children about it. The father, without doubt, was an agreeable man; the woman with him rather reserved than affable, being, as we soon learnt, his sister, come to keep him in order and the children in their place.

notes.text: Your first paragraph gives the new household a mother and a standoffish wife — 'They have… two little kids. The mom is kind of standoffish' — while your third says the father 'is single. Well, divorced.' The same man cannot have both a wife and no wife. I made the standoffish woman his sister, who moved in with him to mind the children: he is a divorced father, and she is not his wife. Then 'single' and 'the mother' both stand, and the discovery of his being single keeps its force.
notes.after: The father, without doubt, was an agreeable man; the woman with him rather reserved than affable, being, as we soon learnt, his sister.

rows.text: My mother lost no time in carrying them biscuits, for she was resolved to learn everything of the family; and what she wished to know was not a little; where they came from, what they did for a living, and whether they went to church.

notes.after: what she wished to know was not a little

rows.text: It was soon found that the father was a lawyer, and that he was single — parted, that is, from his wife; and it was on this intelligence that my mother got a look which I knew exactly how to read. She has been trying to settle me for years, as is natural to a mother whose daughter is not yet settled.

notes.text: A general observation in her manner lays the narrator's dry verdict over the mother's eagerness, saying lightly what the writer only implied.
notes.after: as is natural to a mother whose daughter is not yet settled

lessons: Your passage told a neighbourhood anecdote in nine quick, flat sentences; Austen tells it in a few long, balanced periods, judging character as she goes. I joined your short sentences into two- and four-clause periods ('A new family took the house next door a week since, with a large cart at the door and two young children about it'), named the woman 'rather reserved than affable' where you said 'standoffish', and closed the matter with a dry verdict ('as is natural to a mother whose daughter is not yet settled') instead of stating the mother's design outright. Practise joining clauses with semicolons and letting a late clause carry the point.

outline.gist: A new family moved in next door: a truck, two children
The father seems nice; the mother standoffish
Mother bakes cookies to learn everything about them
The father is a lawyer and single
Mother's design to marry the narrator off

plan.gist: A new family took the house next door, with a large cart and two children
plan.why: News and its furniture first, as she opens a neighbourhood scene

plan.gist: The father agreeable; the woman with him reserved
plan.why: Character judged in her abstract nouns, before any incident

plan.gist: My mother lost no time in taking biscuits, to learn everything
plan.why: Conduct before motive; the point of the visit arrives late in the period

plan.gist: The father proved a lawyer, and not married; the truth of the woman's place at last
plan.why: The discovery that changes the matter, and resolves the sense

plan.gist: My mother's countenance and her long design for me
plan.why: Feeling by conduct, and the narrator's dry verdict to close

sense.problem: Your first sentence gives the new household a mother — 'They have… two little kids. The mom is kind of standoffish' — and your third paragraph says the father 'is single. Well, divorced.' As written, both a wife and no wife are asserted of the same man at the same time.
sense.resolution: Two statements that can both be true are wanted here, not one: let the standoffish woman be someone other than his wife. The least change is to place her as his relative or a member of the household — his sister (or his mother) who moved in with him to help with the children. Then 'single' and 'the mom' both stand: he is a divorced father, and the woman next door is not his wife. Do not make her his ex-wife: a former wife does not move in with him again, and the passage gives no sign of that. Only if she stays his wife must 'single' go.
sense.quote: The mom is kind of standoffish. … It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.

faults.quote: come to keep him in order and the children in their place
faults.why: This invents the sister's purpose and a sharp judgment of her. The writer only said the woman was standoffish. The note reports the sister mending but not this extra characterisation.

faults.quote: as is natural to a mother whose daughter is not yet settled
faults.why: The writer's gender is never given, so 'daughter' is an assumption. The clause also turns the writer's weary exasperation into mild acceptance of the mother, which shifts the feeling.

faults.quote: with a large cart at the door
faults.why: A 'huge truck' becomes a 'large cart', which loses the sense of hugeness. 'At the door' is also added.

faults.quote: what she wished to know was not a little; where they came from, what they did for a living, and whether they went to church.
faults.why: A semicolon before a list that explains the preceding clause reads clumsily, and 'not a little' hangs awkwardly before the list. Austen would use a colon or restructure.

faults.quote: She has been trying to settle me for years, as is natural to a mother whose daughter is not yet settled.
faults.why: The repetition 'settle … settled' is flat and tautological. The sudden present tense after a past-tense narrative is also jarring.

faults.quote: my mother got a look which I knew exactly how to read
faults.why: 'Got a look' is modern colloquial wording kept from the draft. Austen would write 'a look came over my mother's countenance'. The line stays in modern prose dress.

faults.quote: parted, that is, from his wife
faults.why: With the woman already named his sister in paragraph 1, her being 'soon learnt' to be his sister sits oddly with the later 'discovery' that he is single. Some of the turn's force is lost, though the contradiction itself is mended.

faults.quote: cites Emma, ch. 54, ¶ 19
faults.why: This is a precise-looking citation for a phrase ('not a little') that is a generic litotes. The source seems unsupported or invented, and the single move note does not explain why the move works.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: A general observation in her manner lays the narrator's dry verdict over the mother's eagerness
faults.why: The note is vague. It does not flag the invented 'daughter', and it covers none of the other changes: 'keep him in order', cart for truck, the first paragraph's 'without doubt', and the 'week since' rendering.

faults.quote: closed the matter with a dry verdict ('as is natural to a mother whose daughter is not yet settled') instead of stating the mother's design outright
faults.why: The rewrite does state the design outright ('trying to settle me for years'). The lesson also says 'nine quick, flat sentences' when the draft has more, so it misdescribes the text.

faults.quote: the truth of the woman's place at last
faults.why: The outline places the sister reveal at the turn, but the rewrite reveals it in paragraph 1. The 'as the voice would build it' outline therefore does not match the rewrite.

judge.verdict: The rewrite spots and mends the mother/divorced-father contradiction and reports it, and some sentences have an Austen-like balance. It adds inventions ('keep him in order', 'daughter'), has some clumsy or modern phrasing, and its notes and lesson are thin and partly inaccurate.

yours:
Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
Hi team,

The launch is moved from Tuesday to Thursday; for legal has not yet signed off on the pricing page, and I am not willing that we should send it away without that sanction.

I shall be obliged by your having the parts of the deck ready by Wednesday at noon; and if you are stopped in the work, I had rather hear of it today than tomorrow.

Thanks, Sam.

rows.text: Hi team,
The launch is moved from Tuesday to Thursday; for legal has not yet signed off on the pricing page, and I am not willing that we should send it away without that sanction.

notes.after: The launch is moved from Tuesday to Thursday; for legal has not yet signed off on the pricing page, and I am not willing that we should send it away without that sanction.

rows.text: I shall be obliged by your having the parts of the deck ready by Wednesday at noon; and if you are stopped in the work, I had rather hear of it today than tomorrow.

notes.text: the voice turns the bare request into the civil form she gives a favour asked, a courtesy the matter invites but the writer did not say
notes.after: I shall be obliged by

rows.text: Thanks, Sam.

lessons: Your note names each thing plainly and in a hurry; the author's manner holds each clause in a fuller period and lets the civility of the asking carry the firmness of it. The news is given as a completed fact ("is moved") rather than a change in progress, and the reason runs on in one sentence with the refusal of sending ("without that sanction"), where the understatement does the work of a direct "I don't want". Practise so: join the news and its cause in one period with a semicolon, and let a polite turn ("I shall be obliged by") bear a request you once gave as a bare command.

outline.gist: salutation to the team
the launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
legal has not signed off the pricing page; no shipping without it
deck sections due by Wednesday noon
report blocks today, not tomorrow
thanks, signed Sam

plan.gist: salutation to the team
plan.why: a letter keeps its greeting, and hers come first

plan.gist: the launch moves from Tuesday to Thursday
plan.why: the news before the reason, as she gives the matter before its cause

plan.gist: legal unsigned; no sending without it
plan.why: the cause follows, and judgement falls in the third clause

plan.gist: parts of the deck due by Wednesday noon
plan.why: the instruction after its justification

plan.gist: report blocks today, not tomorrow
plan.why: a last short charge, made level by litotes rather than command

plan.gist: thanks and signature
plan.why: the close with thanks in a period of its own

faults.quote: I am not willing that we should send it away without that sanction
faults.why: 'Send it away' is an odd, riddling rendering of 'ship' (it reads as sending the launch away), and 'sanction' for legal sign-off is strained. The sentence is awkward rather than Austenian.

faults.quote: for legal has not yet signed off on the pricing page
faults.why: 'signed off' is modern idiom kept unchanged inside Austen syntax, and 'for' joined after a semicolon is clumsy. The result is modern prose in costume.

faults.quote: I am not willing that we should send it away without that sanction.
faults.why: The writer's 'I don't want us shipping without it' is a mild, personal preference; 'not willing' makes it a firmer refusal. 'Send it away' also shifts the meaning from shipping the product or launch.

faults.quote: I shall be obliged by your having the parts of the deck ready
faults.why: The writer's plain instruction becomes a courteous favour, which softens the directive force. 'Parts' for 'sections' is acceptable but the deck is not 'your having' anything; the phrasing is stilted.

faults.quote: Hi team,
faults.why: The greeting is left in modern casual form, and 'Thanks, Sam.' is also unchanged. The frame stays untranslated, so the rewrite is inconsistent in voice.

faults.quote: if you are stopped in the work, I had rather hear of it today than tomorrow
faults.why: 'Stopped in the work' is vague and not natural idiom for being blocked. The 'today, not tomorrow' contrast loses its urgency as a mild 'had rather'.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
faults.why: The notes are misaligned with the text: the sentence-one move is attributed to 'Paragraph 2', and the greeting paragraph has none. The paragraph numbering is off and the structure of the letter is not reflected.

faults.quote: cites Pride and Prejudice, ch. 47, ¶ 61
faults.why: The citation is a precise-looking, unverifiable source for a generic semicolon-balanced clause; it is not apt and appears invented. The note also calls the sentence 'balanced', which it is not.

faults.quote: [liberty] Liberty taken: the voice turns the bare request into the civil form she gives a favour asked
faults.why: This admits a change of register but does not report the other changes. The 'is moved' tense shift, the softening of 'don't want' and the loss of the 'today, not tomorrow' sharpness go unnoted.

faults.quote: let a polite turn ("I shall be obliged by") bear a request you once gave as a bare command
faults.why: The advice is generic and risky for a work email, where it blunts a deadline. It claims that 'without that sanction' is understatement, which it is not, and it gives no reusable principle with a clear reason.

faults.quote: a last short charge, made level by litotes rather than command
faults.why: The how-it-is-built claims litotes, but the rewrite has none. The 'judgement falls in the third clause' claim and the 'thanks in a period of its own' claim do not match the text, so the outline misdescribes the rewrite.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the facts and order, but its phrasing is awkward ('send it away', 'sanction', 'stopped in the work'), the greeting and sign-off are left modern, and the register shifts the firmness of the requests. The notes and lesson misdescribe the text (nonexistent litotes, misplaced paragraph notes, a dubious citation) and teach little that is reusable.

yours:
Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
It is the opinion of every person of sense in our town that Main Street should be shut against carriages on the days of leisure. The placing of a carriage is a matter of no small difficulty; and the walks, which are too narrow for the little carriages of children, must leave every body pressed and crowded in a way neither safe nor agreeable.

Other places have made the trial, and their shops are doing better than ever they did before.

Some of the shopkeepers will complain, as is usual with such changes, that their customers can no longer get to them; but they will soon be used to it. And, in truth, most people walk from the carriage-house already.

The trial should at least be made this summer.

rows.text: It is the opinion of every person of sense in our town that Main Street should be shut against carriages on the days of leisure. The placing of a carriage is a matter of no small difficulty; and the walks, which are too narrow for the little carriages of children, must leave every body pressed and crowded in a way neither safe nor agreeable.

notes.text: Begins your paragraph 1, which the next paragraph finishes.

notes.after: The placing of a carriage is a matter of no small difficulty; and the walks, which are too narrow for the little carriages of children, must leave every body pressed and crowded in a way neither safe nor agreeable.
a matter of no small difficulty

notes.text: The voice renders the modern word for the weekly holiday by what it is in her world—the days free from business—so the reader knows it at once without a modern name.
notes.after: the days of leisure

rows.text: Other places have made the trial, and their shops are doing better than ever they did before.

notes.text: The rest of your paragraph 1, given a paragraph of its own.

rows.text: Some of the shopkeepers will complain, as is usual with such changes, that their customers can no longer get to them; but they will soon be used to it. And, in truth, most people walk from the carriage-house already.

notes.after: as is usual with such changes

notes.text: A dry generalization the matter itself invites, in the voice's manner: it frames the complaint as the common fate of every alteration, and is the one ironic verdict the passage will bear.
notes.after: as is usual with such changes

rows.text: The trial should at least be made this summer.

lessons: The chief difference is that your passage names each point in a short bare sentence, where the author builds a period that carries the point and its reason in one breath: your two opening sentences become \"The placing of a carriage is a matter of no small difficulty; and the walks... must leave every body pressed and crowded,\" so the complaint arrives already judged. The modern things are rendered by what they do in her world—\"the days of leisure\" for weekends, \"the little carriages of children\" for strollers—so the reader knows them at once without a modern word. Practise holding a reason and its ground together in one balanced sentence, and letting the verdict arrive late, as in \"but they will soon be used to it.\"

outline.gist: The town should close Main Street to carriages on weekends
Parking is difficult and the walks too narrow for carriages
Other places have done it and trade is better
Some shopkeepers will complain customers cannot reach them
They will grow accustomed, and most walk from the carriage-house anyway
Try it this summer

plan.gist: Main Street should be shut to carriages on the days of leisure
plan.why: She opens with the proposal, plainly, in her own period

plan.gist: The difficulty of placing a carriage, and the narrowness of the walks
plan.why: Reason follows the claim as it does in her arguments, joined in one period

plan.gist: Other places have tried it and found their trade increase
plan.why: The evidence before the objection, as she orders a case

plan.gist: The complaint of the shopkeepers, and the answer that custom will reconcile them
plan.why: Objection and answer in one paragraph, the objection reported, the answer a verdict

plan.gist: Most people walk from the carriage-house
plan.why: The decisive point kept last in its paragraph, as she places the strongest where it lands

plan.gist: The trial should be made in the summer
plan.why: A short closing sentence as a verdict, the proposal renewed

faults.quote: It is the opinion of every person of sense in our town that
faults.why: The writer's plain proposal becomes a claim that every sensible person agrees. This adds a consensus the writer never asserted. It also turns the writer's "we should" into an impersonal appeal. The notes do not report it.

faults.quote: must leave every body pressed and crowded in a way neither safe nor agreeable
faults.why: The writer said only that the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. The rewrite adds crowding for everyone and a safety danger, which are new claims. The notes do not report them.

faults.quote: The placing of a carriage is a matter of no small difficulty
faults.why: The writer's "nightmare" is flattened into mild litotes, and "downtown" is lost. Litotes is an Austen move, but here it weakens the feeling's degree. The notes do not acknowledge the shift.

faults.quote: The trial should at least be made this summer.
faults.why: "At least" is added and the writer's "We should try it" becomes impersonal. This softens the call to action slightly. "Honestly" is also dropped from the shopkeeper paragraph and its emphasis lost.

faults.quote: too narrow for the little carriages of children, must leave
faults.why: "Carriages" now means both the vehicles being banned and the strollers. A reader may be confused or amused, and the rewrite does not guard against it.

faults.quote: The placing of a carriage
faults.why: A clumsy modern gerund for "parking". Austen would not say it this way. It reads like a translation rather than her idiom.

faults.quote: on the days of leisure
faults.why: This is a vague, invented periphrasis for "weekends". It does not tell the reader which days are meant, and it blurs the proposal. The note justifies it as "days free from business", which is not what Austen's usage supports.

faults.quote: cites Emma, ch. 3, ¶ 5
faults.why: The citations (Emma, Sense and Sensibility, Northanger Abbey) are attached to the rewrite's own phrases as if they were sources. They are loosely apt at best and not verifiable. The notes also leave out the added "every person of sense" and "neither safe nor agreeable".

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: The closing paragraph changed the writer's "We should try it" to an impersonal "at least" construction, and nothing is reported.

faults.quote: Other places have made the trial, and their shops are doing better than ever they did before.
faults.why: Plausibly Austen-like, but the evidence is left as a bare, flat one-sentence paragraph. There is no ironic or evaluative turn of the kind the voice would use.

faults.quote: your two opening sentences become
faults.why: The lesson says the writer's two opening sentences became one period. The opening sentence of the rewrite is actually the added "It is the opinion..." line, so the lesson's account is partly inaccurate. The lesson also centres on one move, the long balanced period, rather than several.

judge.verdict: A competent, mostly faithful Austenian rewrite with a sensible structure. It adds unreported claims (universal opinion, safety), softens "nightmare", and creates a carriage/stroller ambiguity. The voice is only moderately convincing, and the notes and lesson are thin and slightly inaccurate.

yours:
I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I think we should shorten the week to four days, for our people are worn out with their labour, and the best hand among them has this week quitted his place. There have been accounts, I believe, which shew that the work done does not fall off under such an arrangement, but holds its ground or rather mends. It would likewise be of service in engaging new people, which is no small matter in the present scarcity; and I own it, the scheme has its hazards, and our employers might not look upon it kindly.

But we might make trial of it for three months, and then stand convicted or acquitted by the event.

rows.text: I think we should shorten the week to four days, for our people are worn out with their labour, and the best hand among them has this week quitted his place. There have been accounts, I believe, which shew that the work done does not fall off under such an arrangement, but holds its ground or rather mends. It would likewise be of service in engaging new people, which is no small matter in the present scarcity; and I own it, the scheme has its hazards, and our employers might not look upon it kindly.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.

notes.after: which is no small matter in the present scarcity

notes.text: the narrator grants the risk in her own dry phrase, letting the concession carry the weight of an honest admission rather than a bare statement

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

And it came to pass at midnight, that Ryan sent unto me, saying, We must talk together. And I knew straightway what that meant.

And I would have wept, but I wept not; and I bowed my head and said, It is well. Then I walked home in the rain, and did eat a whole measure of ice cream.

And my friend that dwelleth with me judged that I made too much thereof; and peradventure I did. But it hurt me still.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
And it came to pass that a new family took the house beside ours, with a great truck, and with them two little children. The man of the house seemeth pleasant, and his sister holdeth herself aloof.

And my mother straightway baked them cakes, and went over that she might learn all that might be learned of them: whence they came, and what work they did, and whether they went to church.

And it was found that the man was a lawyer, and he was single; nay, he was divorced. And my mother set this look upon her face, and I knew right well what she was thinking: for she hath sought these many years to set me up.

notes.text: Nothing else in the passage cannot be true of the same people; no time or person is unclear beyond the above. No scene of the author's is truly echoed here (no prodigal return, no stranger's mercy, no flight from a charge, no refusal to part, no envious brothers, no ordered season). Nothing is mended and nothing is echoed; the rewrite leaves it be.

Your second paragraph gives the newcomers a mother and a father together: 'The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.' Your fourth paragraph then says 'the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.' A household cannot have both a mother living in it and a single (if divorced) father as its only parent: the reader cannot tell whether the 'mom' is a second adult, a former wife still present, or someone else. I made the 'mom' the man's sister, not his wife: another of his household for whom 'mom' was a slip. That keeps both sentences true at once, and the cookies, the two children and the matchmaking all stand. Least change: one noun.
notes.after: The man of the house seemeth pleasant, and his sister holdeth herself aloof.

faults.quote: if thou art hindered

faults.quote: (no notes)

faults.quote: and I would not have us ship without it

Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
And it were well for our town that Main Street be shut unto heaps upon the days of rest, and that men leave their wagons without the gate. For the laying of wagons in the midst of the town is a sore vexation, and the walks are too narrow, that carriages may not pass therein: for strait is the way, and narrow is the path thereof.

And other towns have done this thing, and their booths prosper more than before: better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof.

Yet some that keep shops will murmur, saying, Our guests cannot come unto us. But they shall be accustomed unto it in a little while. For the greater part of men walk from the store even as it is; yea, they do so even now.

lessons: Your page states a case in short modern sentences, one clause to each; the author lays clause beside clause with "and," half of its sentences running far longer, and turns each new matter with "And" or "Yet" or "Wherefore." Practise joining two small thoughts into one long sentence ("And other towns have done this thing, and their booths prosper more than before"), and giving feeling and fact through settled verdicts like "better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof," which closes the evidence on the cadence of the author rather than on the bare claim.

other towns did it, shops better

faults.quote: shut unto heaps
faults.why: Garbled rendering of 'closed to cars'. 'Heaps' is meaningless here, and the idea of cars is lost.

faults.quote: the walks are too narrow, that carriages may not pass therein: for strait is the way, and narrow is the path thereof.
faults.why: The writer said sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. This turns it into carriages being unable to pass, and 'strait is the way' adds a redundant, scriptural-sounding tautology. The stroller point is distorted.

faults.quote: better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof
faults.why: Invented proverb with no basis in the draft. It is an added claim, and it misfits the point that the shops are doing better than ever.

faults.quote: For the greater part of men walk from the store even as it is; yea, they do so even now.
faults.why: 'Garage' becomes 'store', which is nonsense. The sentence also repeats itself with 'yea, they do so even now'. 'Honestly' is lost.

faults.quote: Our guests cannot come unto us.
faults.why: 'Customers' becomes 'guests', a slight shift in meaning. 'Their shops are doing better than ever' is softened to 'prosper more than before'.

faults.quote: For the greater part of men walk from the store
faults.why: The garage-to-shop reasoning is broken, so the answer to the objection no longer makes sense. It fails to carry the point that most already walk from the garage.

faults.quote: But they shall be accustomed unto it in a little while.
faults.why: 'Be accustomed unto' is not KJV idiom, and the phrase reads awkwardly. 'Shut unto heaps' and 'booths' (for shops) also read as garble.

faults.quote: men leave their wagons without the gate
faults.why: Anachronistic substitution of wagons and a gate for cars and downtown. The result reads as costume rather than idiom.

faults.quote: cites 2 Kings 10:8
faults.why: The cited verse is about heaps at the gate, which is irrelevant to the move claimed ('clauses laid side by side with and'). The move name and the source do not match.

faults.quote: cites Proverbs 23:27
faults.why: Parallelism claimed, but the cited verse (a deep ditch) does not illustrate it. The quoted sentence is not really parallelism.

faults.quote: cites Genesis 41:56

faults.quote: Structure: Begins your paragraph 1, which the next paragraph finishes.
faults.why: The rewrite splits the writer's paragraph 1 for no stated reason, and this is a bare description with no explanation. Paragraph 4 has no notes, and the invented proverb and the changes to meaning go unreported.

faults.quote: Paragraph 2 (renders the writer’s ¶1):
faults.why: The split of the first paragraph leaves the evidence sentence stranded. The argument's claim and reasons are not clearly separated, and the objection and answer lose force because the answer is muddled.

faults.quote: giving feeling and fact through settled verdicts like "better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof,"
faults.why: Teaches the writer to add an invented proverb that changes the meaning and is not in the text. It is a poor model and does not teach anything reusable about argument structure.

faults.quote: And it were well for our town
faults.why: 'And it were well' is an odd, semi-archaic subjunctive that is not KJV. Opening every paragraph with 'And' or 'Yet' is a thin imitation of the real cadence.

I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I think we should turn unto a week of four days: for the people are spent with labour, and the chief of our builders is departed from us. And there be works which shew that the work of the people abideth the same, or is increased, when the days are fewer. And it should avail us also for the taking of men unto the work.

I know that it is perilous, and that our clients may be ill pleased therewith. Yet let us prove it for the space of three months, and behold what cometh of it.

rows.text: I think we should turn unto a week of four days: for the people are spent with labour, and the chief of our builders is departed from us. And there be works which shew that the work of the people abideth the same, or is increased, when the days are fewer. And it should avail us also for the taking of men unto the work.

notes.after: the taking of men unto the work
turn unto a week of four days

rows.text: I know that it is perilous, and that our clients may be ill pleased therewith. Yet let us prove it for the space of three months, and behold what cometh of it.

notes.after: and behold what cometh of it

lessons: Their passage is a terse office pitch; the author's voice turns each point into a full sentence of balanced clauses, opened with And and joined by colons, so the argument moves gravely from judgment to proof to doubt to trial. Practise laying clause beside clause with and, as in "for the people are spent with labour, and the chief of our builders is departed from us", and saying a thing twice in parallel halves, as in "abideth the same, or is increased"; both slow the reader down and give the claim the weight of a verdict rather than a memo.

reading.kind: argument (a pitch for a change at work, first person)

outline.gist: we should move to a four-day week
people are burned out and the best engineer quit
studies show output holds or rises
it would also help hiring
it is risky and clients may not like it
try it three months and see

plan.gist: the move to a four-day week
plan.why: The voice opens with the judgment, plainly: what should be done.

plan.gist: men are spent, and the best of the builders is gone
plan.why: The occasion demands the trouble be named first, as the cause of the judgment.

plan.gist: the works shew the labour holdeth or groweth
plan.why: Proof follows the need, laid beside it with and.

plan.gist: it availeth also for the taking of men
plan.why: A further good, added before the doubt, that the case stand full.

plan.gist: I know it is perilous, and the clients may be displeased
plan.why: The danger is confessed before the answer, that the answer may carry more weight.

plan.gist: let us prove it three months and behold
plan.why: A short trial is the voice's way out: do it, and see.

faults.quote: the people are spent with labour
faults.why: The writer said 'burned out'. 'Spent with labour' keeps burnout but shifts it to ordinary tiredness from work, so it is slightly weaker.

faults.quote: And there be works which shew that the work of the people abideth the same
faults.why: 'Studies' becomes 'works', which is ambiguous in KJV diction. 'Works' also repeats in 'the work of the people', which is clumsy. The writer's 'or goes up' is kept, but 'when the days are fewer' is added as a condition.

faults.quote: the chief of our builders is departed from us
faults.why: 'Our best engineer' becomes 'the chief of our builders'. 'Chief' suggests rank rather than skill, and the writer's 'quit' is softened to 'departed'.

faults.quote: for the people are spent with labour
faults.why: The writer states the burnout and the quitting as plain reasons. The 'for' makes them the cause of the claim, which is acceptable, but 'the chief ... is departed' is attached to the same 'for', so the engineer's quitting reads as an effect of the labour rather than a separate reason.

faults.quote: I think we should turn unto a week of four days
faults.why: 'I think we should' is modern. The KJV would say 'Let us' or 'It is meet that we'. 'Turn unto a week' is also not an idiom the KJV uses.

faults.quote: And it should avail us also for the taking of men unto the work.
faults.why: 'Should avail' is modern modal phrasing, not the KJV's 'shall' or 'availeth'. 'Taking of men unto the work' is awkward and stilted rather than idiomatic.

faults.quote: the taking of men unto the work
faults.why: 'Taking' for hiring is obscure and could be read as seizing or conscripting, and 'the work' is vague.

faults.quote: our clients may be ill pleased therewith
faults.why: 'Ill pleased' is plausible, but 'may' is modern. The KJV would use 'peradventure' or 'it may be that'.

faults.quote: cites Ephesians 6:16
faults.why: Ephesians 6:16 is about the shield of faith and quenching fiery darts. It has no relation to a genitive 'of' construction, so the source is inapt.

faults.quote: cites Haggai 2:20
faults.why: This verse is not a clear example of 'turn unto' or 'thereof', so the citation is questionable and does not demonstrate the move named.

faults.quote: cites Genesis 37:19
faults.why: Genesis 37:19 reads 'Behold, this dreamer cometh', which supports 'behold', but not 'lo, verily'. The notes are thin overall, with only three entries and nothing on the 'for', 'And' or parallelism moves that the lesson claims.

faults.quote: opened with And and joined by colons
faults.why: The lesson says the rewrite is 'opened with And' and joined by colons, but only one sentence begins with 'And' and there is a single colon. It also says 'balanced clauses' while the 'saying a thing twice' example is a mild pairing ('abideth the same, or is increased') that is not real parallelism.

faults.quote: Yet let us prove it for the space of three months, and behold what cometh of it.
faults.why: The structure is kept, but the outline claims the voice would open with the judgment, as the rewrite does, and does not note that the benefit comes after the evidence. The notes do not explain that no order was changed.

judge.verdict: A competent, faithful archaizing rewrite that keeps every element, but some diction is modern or obscure ('should avail', 'taking of men', 'works') and the notes cite mismatched verses. The lesson overstates the colons and 'And' openings.

When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
And it came to pass that Dana put off our dinner unto another day; and I was not grieved at all. In truth, I was relieved; for I had feared it all the week, and I am not proud that it was so.

And I said unto her, It is well, and another time we shall sup together. Yet I do not think it shall be; neither is it in my heart that it shall be.

rows.text: And it came to pass that Dana put off our dinner unto another day; and I was not grieved at all. In truth, I was relieved; for I had feared it all the week, and I am not proud that it was so.

notes.after: And it came to pass that Dana put off our dinner unto another day; and I was not grieved at all.
In truth, I was relieved; for I had feared it all the week, and I am not proud that it was so.
Dana put off our dinner unto another day

notes.text: the writer's plain confession of shame, given the Bible's grave naming of inward fault against oneself: the voice judges what the writer already owns
notes.after: and I am not proud that it was so

rows.text: And I said unto her, It is well, and another time we shall sup together. Yet I do not think it shall be; neither is it in my heart that it shall be.

notes.technique: Clauses laid side by side with “and”
notes.after: And I said unto her, It is well, and another time we shall sup together.
And I said unto her, It is well

notes.text: the writer's doubt turned into the narrator's inward word, a verdict the passage itself points to at its close
notes.after: neither is it in my heart that it shall be

lessons: Your passage is a private confession told in five short modern breaths; the Bible's manner is to join each turn with "and" and to give feeling by its sign, so I laid the deed, the relief, and the shame side by side ("and I was not grieved at all; in truth, I was relieved"). The close sets outward speech against inward doubt in two balanced halves ("Yet I do not think it shall be; neither is it in my heart that it shall be"), which is the parallelism to practise: say the thing once, then say its other half.

felt relief, honestly
had feared it all week; not proud
said it was fine, another time
do not think another time will come

plan.gist: Dana puts off the dinner
plan.why: the story opens on the deed that changes things, as the Bible opens a turn with what befell

plan.gist: no sorrow, but relief
plan.why: the heart's answer follows the deed at once, told plainly and gravely

plan.gist: the dread of the week, and shame at it
plan.why: the narrator's inward truth, set against the verdict before it

plan.gist: the word given Dana, and the hidden thought
plan.why: speech then inward doubt, the outward and inward halves of the same turn, ending where it lands hardest

faults.quote: neither is it in my heart that it shall be
faults.why: This adds a new clause about the heart. The writer only said 'I don't think we will'. It turns doubt into an inward disposition or refusal, which shifts the feeling toward intent. The notes admit it as a 'liberty', but it is an addition.

faults.quote: put off our dinner unto another day
faults.why: The writer said 'cancelled'. 'Put off unto another day' implies an explicit rescheduling that did not happen, and it pre-empts the later line about doing it 'another time'.

faults.quote: I was not grieved at all
faults.why: 'Not upset' becomes 'not grieved', which is a heavier word and slightly shifts the register of the feeling.

faults.quote: I had feared it all the week
faults.why: 'Dreading' becomes 'feared', which is weaker in sense. 'All the week' is modern phrasing, and the KJV would say 'all the week long' or 'all the days of the week'. It reads as costume.

faults.quote: another time we shall sup together
faults.why: 'Sup together' is a quaint rendering of 'do it another time'. The 'shall' of promise does not quite match the casual 'we'd do it another time', which was a polite soft remark.

faults.quote: I am not proud that it was so
faults.why: The tense is mixed and the phrasing is stiff. A KJV-style rendering would more naturally be 'and I am ashamed' or similar. It also loses the flat modern understatement.

faults.quote: cites Ruth 3:8
faults.why: The citations seem arbitrary. Psalms 94:23 is cited for 'unto', and Psalms 119:51 for a parallelism that the line does not actually contain. The cited verses do not demonstrate the moves named, and 'thereof, wherefore' are listed but not used.

faults.quote: the writer's plain confession of shame, given the Bible's grave naming of inward fault against oneself: the voice judges what the writer already owns
faults.why: This is muddled and vague. It claims a liberty the rewrite barely took, and the explanation is unclear.

faults.quote: say the thing once, then say its other half
faults.why: The lesson is partly inaccurate. The closing 'Yet I do not think it shall be; neither...' is mere repetition rather than true parallelism, and the claim that it balances outward speech against inward doubt is overstated. It also claims the passage was joined by 'and' throughout, but only some sentences were.

faults.quote: Yet I do not think it shall be
faults.why: 'Do not think' with a 'do' auxiliary is not KJV-typical, which prefers 'I think not'. The line is a hybrid of modern and archaic.

judge.verdict: A competent but thin KJV pastiche: the opening is recognisably in manner, but the ending adds an invented 'heart' clause, and the notes cite sources that do not fit the moves named. The lesson overstates what the rewrite achieved.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan sent me a message at midnight, and he said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant, because it's the kind of message nobody sends when the news is good.

The next day we met at a small place downtown, and he was already there when I walked in, his eyes on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious, and then he said the rest of it: it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry, but I held it in, and I just said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and took in a whole carton of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was making too much of it, and maybe I was. But it still hurt.

rows.text: Ryan sent me a message at midnight, and he said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant, because it's the kind of message nobody sends when the news is good.

notes.text: the voice frames what the writer leaves implied, in plain words; it turns the detail into a small verdict that sets the reader up for the hurt to come.
notes.after: the kind of message nobody sends when the news is good

rows.text: The next day we met at a small place downtown, and he was already there when I walked in, his eyes on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious, and then he said the rest of it: it wasn't me, it was him.
I wanted to cry, but I held it in, and I just said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and took in a whole carton of ice cream.
My roommate thought I was making too much of it, and maybe I was. But it still hurt.

lessons: The writer's draft moves in very short, staccato sentences, one small fact per line; Obama joins those into longer, balanced sentences spoken aloud, so the midnight message and its meaning come together, and each paragraph lands on a heavier beat. Practise the turn I made with "But it still hurt": let the whole paragraph build to a short verdict, the shortest sentence set against the longest, so the reader feels the weight of it. Notice also how the plain framing — "the kind of message nobody sends when the news is good" — lets one detail stand for the whole thing, which is what makes a small story stay with someone.

outline.gist: midnight message asking to talk
meeting downtown, him nervous, the breakup reasons
holding it in, walking home in the rain with ice cream
roommate doubts, maybe so, but it still hurt

plan.gist: the midnight message and what it meant
plan.why: start with the single detail that sets the whole thing in motion, and let one moment stand for what is coming

plan.gist: the downtown meeting and the words he used
plan.why: set the scene plainly, then give the words as reported speech, fair to him even in the hurt

plan.gist: keeping it together, the walk home, the small comfort of ice cream
plan.why: particular and unadorned; the grief shown, not announced

plan.gist: the roommate's doubt, and the turn to the simple truth
plan.why: end on antithesis and the plain fact that it still hurt: not a slogan, just the truth

faults.quote: because it's the kind of message nobody sends when the news is good
faults.why: Adds a new claim and explanation that the writer did not make; the writer only said they knew what it meant. It is an added commentary sentence that goes beyond mere voice-framing, and it is reported only vaguely as a 'liberty'.

faults.quote: and then he said the rest of it: it wasn't me, it was him.
faults.why: 'the rest of it' adds a slight rhetorical build that was not in the draft. It changes the sequence into a reveal and adds a mild editorial tone.

faults.quote: I held it in, and I just said okay
faults.why: The writer said 'I just nodded and said okay'. The nod is dropped, which is a small loss of fact.

faults.quote: took in a whole carton of ice cream
faults.why: The writer wrote 'a whole pint'. 'Carton' changes the quantity detail. 'Ate' became 'took in', a stilted word.

faults.quote: Ryan sent me a message at midnight, and he said we needed to talk.
faults.why: This is largely the draft with conjunctions joined; it lacks Obama's signature moves: reflective first-person asides, 'Now,' 'Look,' triadic rhythm, a wider-lens reflection, self-deprecating humor, or a universal turn. It reads as lightly polished modern prose, not Obama.

faults.quote: My roommate thought I was making too much of it, and maybe I was. But it still hurt.
faults.why: Almost identical to the original; the antithesis is Obama-like in shape but nothing is built to make it land, and the lesson claims a long-to-short build that the paragraph does not actually deliver.

faults.quote: at a small place downtown
faults.why: 'Small place' is vaguer than 'coffee shop' and loses the concrete detail; also 'his eyes on his phone' is fine, but 'took in' for eating is awkward.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 2:
  (no notes)
faults.why: Paragraphs 2–4 have no notes, though changes were made (coffee shop to 'small place', 'scrolling' to 'eyes on his phone', dropped nod, 'ate' to 'took in', 'overreacting' to 'making too much of it'). Only one vague note is given, and it does not name a source or a concrete move.

faults.quote: [liberty] Liberty taken: the voice frames what the writer leaves implied
faults.why: Note is generic and does not cite any Obama text or speech; it also describes the added clause as framing when it is an invented generalization.

faults.quote: Practise the turn I made with "But it still hurt"
faults.why: The writer's own text already had this line unchanged, so the lesson credits the rewriter with a move the writer already made. It is misleading and not transferable.

faults.quote: Obama joins those into longer, balanced sentences spoken aloud
faults.why: The claim is generic and the rewrite barely does it; the outline's 'reported speech' and 'antithesis' claims are not reflected in the text, which still has direct 'it wasn't me, it was him'.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is a light touch-up of the draft with one invented generalization and a few small changes (dropped nod, pint to carton), and it hardly sounds like Obama. The notes are thin and the lesson credits moves that were already in the original or are not actually present.

rewrite:
A new family moved in next door last weekend, a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom — the kids’ mom, the dad’s ex — is kind of standoffish.

My mother put together a batch of cookies for them right away. She wanted to find out everything about them — where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he’s single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.

rows.text: A new family moved in next door last weekend, a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom — the kids’ mom, the dad’s ex — is kind of standoffish.

notes.text: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother (“The mom is kind of standoffish”), and a few sentences later says the dad “is single.” As written, the same household has a mother and a single father, which can’t both be true of the same pair — and nothing tells the reader who the woman is. I made the woman’s place plain: she is the children’s mother and the dad’s former wife, not a partner now, so the household keeps a mother, the dad stays single and divorced, and the two sentences agree.
notes.after: The mom — the kids’ mom, the dad’s ex — is kind of standoffish.

rows.text: My mother put together a batch of cookies for them right away. She wanted to find out everything about them — where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.
It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he’s single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.

lessons: Your draft tells the story in short, bare sentences; Obama builds each sentence out of balanced clauses with “, and” so the narration flows as if spoken, and lets the short sentence land only as a turn or verdict. Notice how “My mom got this look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking” joins two beats into one spoken cadence, and how the three questions (“where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church”) build to a single point. Practise joining your short sentences with “, and” and saving the brief sentence for the turn that matters.

outline.gist: new family moved in next door, truck, two kids
dad nice, mom standoffish
mother baked cookies, want to learn everything about them
dad is lawyer and single, divorced
mom's look, trying to set narrator up

plan.gist: new family next door, the truck and kids
plan.why: The voice opens with the particular detail that stands for the whole, planting the scene plainly before anything is judged.

plan.gist: the dad seems nice; the mom his former wife, standoffish
plan.why: One line each, balanced with the antithesis the voice favours; the mend makes the mother's place plain so the later 'single' agrees.

plan.gist: mother baked cookies right away, wanted to find out everything
plan.why: The story of one person's welcome, then the turn from what happened to what it means — the mother's wanting to know them.

plan.gist: dad is a lawyer, single — well, divorced
plan.why: The news before the verdict; the 'well' turns the sentence on the voice's correction, and lands where it counts.

plan.gist: mom's look, knowing what she was thinking, years of setup
plan.why: The paragraph lands on the narrator's reading of the look and what it means for what comes next, closing with the threes of her effort.

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother ("The mom is kind of standoffish"), and a few sentences later says the dad "is single." As written, the same household has a mother and a single father, which can't both be true of the same pair — and nothing tells the reader who the woman is.
sense.resolution: Keep everything as is, but make the woman's place in the household plain: she is the children's mother and the dad's former wife, not a partner now — e.g. "The mom — the kids' mom, the dad's ex — is kind of standoffish." That mends it with the least change: the family keeps a mother, the dad stays single and divorced, and the reader is given only the step needed to make the two sentences agree.
sense.quote: The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish. … It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.

faults.quote: The mom — the kids’ mom, the dad’s ex — is kind of standoffish.
faults.why: The mend makes the ex-wife part of the household that just moved in next door, which is implausible. A divorced couple living together is a new puzzle, and it undercuts the mother's matchmaking hope. The more natural mend is that the woman is someone else in the household (a sister, the dad's mother, a girlfriend, a nanny). The note does not explain why the ex lives there.

faults.quote: the kids’ mom, the dad’s ex
faults.why: This invents facts the writer never gave: that the woman is the children's mother and the dad's former wife. The note presents it as a clarification and does not flag it as a guess.

faults.quote: A new family moved in next door last weekend, a huge truck and two little kids.
faults.why: Merging the sentences turns 'They have a huge truck' into an appositive that reads as if the family consists of a truck and kids. The possession is lost and the line is slightly garbled.

faults.quote: The mom — the kids’ mom, the dad’s ex — is kind of standoffish.
faults.why: The stacked, self-correcting dashes read as clumsy, and the 'ex' tag lands before the later 'Well, divorced' reveal. That spoils the reveal's timing and its small turn.

faults.quote: My mother put together a batch of cookies for them
faults.why: This replaces 'baked them cookies' with a vaguer phrase. It changes the writer's detail for no gain and may suggest the cookies were not baked.

faults.quote: My mom got this look on her face, and I knew exactly what she was thinking.
faults.why: The rewrite is almost the draft with a few joins and dashes. It has little of Obama's cadence, such as rhetorical balance, wry self-aware asides, or longer periodic sentences. It reads as the original with light edits, not as modern prose rendered in his manner.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 2:
  (no notes)
Paragraph 3:
  (no notes)
faults.why: Changes were made in both paragraphs (the 'baked' to 'put together' swap, merged sentences, and added punctuation), but none are noted. There are no moves with sources, so the writer cannot see what was altered.

faults.quote: The voice opens with the particular detail that stands for the whole... balanced with the antithesis the voice favours... closing with the threes of her effort.
faults.why: The structure notes claim Obama-like moves (antithesis, a close on 'threes of her effort') that are not in the rewrite. The three-part list was already in the draft, and the ending is the draft's own line.

faults.quote: Obama builds each sentence out of balanced clauses with “, and” so the narration flows as if spoken
faults.why: The lesson is generic and overstated. It credits Obama with a move the rewrite barely makes (one merged sentence) and credits him with the three questions, which the writer already wrote. The writer gains little transferable and no reason why the move works. It also ignores the real lesson about the contradiction.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is a near-copy of the draft with light punctuation changes, so the Obama voice is faint. The sense mend invents an implausible ex-wife living with the dad, and the notes and lesson claim moves that are not in the text.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

rewrite:

A quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the page that sets out our prices, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your parts of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

rows.text: Hi team,
A quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the page that sets out our prices, and I don't want us shipping without it.
Please have your parts of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.
Thanks, Sam

lessons: The writer's note is terse and imperative; Obama's manner leads with the news plainly, then gives the reason, then asks. The rewrite turns "I don't want us shipping without it" into a shared standard ("us"), and frames the second request as a simple antithesis ("today, not tomorrow") that lands with his caution. Practise the turn from news to reason to request, and let the "we" carry the weight the writer's "I" carried alone.

Launch moved from Tuesday to Thursday
Legal hasn't signed off on pricing page; don't want to ship without it
Sections of deck due Wednesday noon
Tell me today if blocked, not tomorrow
Thanks, Sam

plan.gist: Hi team
plan.why: Keep the greeting simple and direct, the way Obama opens.

plan.gist: The launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday
plan.why: Lead with the news, plainly, before the reason.

plan.gist: Legal hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and we shouldn't ship without it
plan.why: Give the reason right after the news, so the team understands the change.

plan.gist: Send your parts of the deck by Wednesday noon
plan.why: The request follows the reason, turning to what each person must do.

plan.gist: If anything is blocking you, tell me today, not tomorrow
plan.why: Put the second request last, where it lands as caution rather than command.

plan.gist: Thanks, Sam
plan.why: Close with thanks, as Obama closes addresses.

faults.quote: A quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday.
faults.why: Nearly identical to the original; only an article was added. No Obama cadence (a framing clause, a 'look' or 'here's the thing', a rhythmic triad, a 'we'). It reads as the writer's own prose.

faults.quote: the page that sets out our prices
faults.why: The only real change is a periphrasis of 'pricing page'. It is wordier and no more Obama-like. It sounds slightly stilted for a work email.

faults.quote: Please have your parts of the deck done by Wednesday at noon.
faults.why: Only 'sections' became 'parts', a trivial and arguably weaker swap. There is no Obama move such as a shared-effort framing or a rhetorical balance.

faults.quote: Thanks, Sam
faults.why: The sign-off was collapsed to one line, which is a trivial formatting change and not a voice move. The 'Hi team' greeting remains modern-casual.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
faults.why: All four paragraphs have no notes, even though words were changed ('sections' to 'parts', 'pricing page' to 'page that sets out our prices', 'Quick' to 'A quick'). The changes are unreported and no moves are named with sources.

faults.quote: The rewrite turns "I don't want us shipping without it" into a shared standard ("us")
faults.why: The lesson claims a change that did not happen. The rewrite kept 'I don't want us shipping without it' word for word, and 'us' was already in the original.

faults.quote: frames the second request as a simple antithesis ("today, not tomorrow")
faults.why: The antithesis is the writer's own, unchanged. The lesson credits the rewrite with something it did not do.

faults.quote: Legal hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and we shouldn't ship without it.
faults.why: The outline claims the voice would change 'I don't want us' to 'we shouldn't', but the rewrite did not do this. The outline and the text disagree, and the stated reordering of the closing request is not reflected either.

faults.quote: Practise the turn from news to reason to request, and let the "we" carry the weight the writer's "I" carried alone.
faults.why: The writer's order was already news, reason, request, so there is nothing to learn from a turn the rewrite did not make. The 'we' advice does not match the text, because the 'I' is still there. The lesson is generic and untrue to the rewrite.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is essentially the original with two trivial word swaps. It has no real Obama voice, and the notes and lesson describe changes that were never made. Meaning is preserved, but the tool delivers almost nothing as a voice rewrite or as teaching.

Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Our town should close Main Street to cars on the weekends. Here's the thing: parking downtown is a nightmare, and the walks are too narrow for a stroller.

Other towns have done it, and their shops are doing better than ever.

Now, some business owners will tell you their customers won't be able to get to them. But they'll get used to it. The truth is, most folks walk over from the garage anyway.

And that's why we should try it this summer.

rows.text: Our town should close Main Street to cars on the weekends. Here's the thing: parking downtown is a nightmare, and the walks are too narrow for a stroller.

notes.text: Begins your paragraph 1, which the next paragraph finishes.

notes.after: Here's the thing: parking downtown is a nightmare, and the walks are too narrow for a stroller.

rows.text: Other towns have done it, and their shops are doing better than ever.

notes.text: The rest of your paragraph 1, given a paragraph of its own.

rows.text: Now, some business owners will tell you their customers won't be able to get to them. But they'll get used to it. The truth is, most folks walk over from the garage anyway.
And that's why we should try it this summer.

notes.technique: From what happened to what we do
notes.after: And that's why we should try it this summer.

lessons: The biggest change is how the piece is built as speech: the proposal leads, then the problem on the ground, then the proof from other towns, then the objection named and answered, and it all lands on a "that's why" turn. Notice the plain address ("Here's the thing," "The truth is") and the shared "we" ("we should try it this summer") — speaking directly to the listener and closing on what we do together makes the ask feel like ours, not just the writer's.

outline.gist: Close Main Street to cars on weekends
Parking is a nightmare, sidewalks too narrow for strollers
Other towns did it, shops doing better
Some owners will complain customers can't reach them
They'll get used to it
Most people walk from the garage anyway
Let's try it this summer

plan.gist: Open with the proposal, plainly, as the thing we should do
plan.why: Obama leads with the clear ask, in the shared 'we' — says what we should do before giving the reasons

plan.gist: Then the problem on the ground: parking and narrow walks
plan.why: The particular difficulty first, so the listener feels it before the answer

plan.gist: The turn: other towns have done this, and their shops are better for it
plan.why: One town's story stands for many; the proof comes before the objection it answers

plan.gist: Name the worry some owners will raise, and answer it plainly; most walk anyway
plan.why: Be fair to everyone, then settle it — not this fear, but the truth of how people actually get downtown

plan.gist: Land on the ask: let's try it this summer
plan.why: Close on what comes next, the shared 'we' set in motion

faults.quote: the walks are too narrow for a stroller
faults.why: The writer said 'sidewalks' and 'strollers' (plural). 'Walks' is an odd clipped substitute, and the singular changes the meaning slightly.

faults.quote: the walks are too narrow
faults.why: 'Walks' is not idiomatic for sidewalks, and Obama would say 'sidewalks'. It reads as a garble.

faults.quote: And that's why we should try it this summer.
faults.why: 'That's why' implies the preceding sentence is the cause. The writer's call was a plain ask, and the false causal link makes a non sequitur after the walking point.

faults.quote: Now, some business owners will tell you their customers won't be able to get to them.
faults.why: The objection is concessive in the Obama manner, but the answer ('they'll get used to it') stays blunt and dismissive. There is no fair-minded acknowledgment of the owners' worry, no 'I understand', and no turn to the shared 'we'.

faults.quote: But they'll get used to it.
faults.why: This is kept verbatim from the draft and is flat and dismissive. The real voice would temper or build the answer, so it reads as the writer's prose with a few Obama tags added.

faults.quote: Our town should close Main Street to cars on the weekends.
faults.why: Almost unchanged from the draft. Overall the rewrite is a light touch-up with 'Here's the thing', 'Now', and 'The truth is' sprinkled on, lacking Obama's rhythm, tricolon, or anecdote cadence.

faults.quote: Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.
faults.why: The rewrite does not fix the weak logic of the answer. Walking from the garage does not address customers who can't drive up to the shop, and the note does not flag it.

faults.quote: Structure: Begins your paragraph 1, which the next paragraph finishes.
faults.why: This describes a paragraph split but not why. It is a mechanical remark rather than a real structural explanation.

faults.quote: cites Weekly Address, 8 June 2013, ¶ 8
faults.why: A 'that's why' closing is claimed as 'from what happened to what we do', but here nothing has happened that leads to it. The citation is not apt, and 'The truth is' has no note at all.

faults.quote: Other towns have done it, and their shops are doing better than ever.
faults.why: It is split into its own paragraph, which is trivial. The 'how it is built' claims a reordering and the 'turn', yet the rewrite keeps the writer's order exactly, so the outline and the rewrite do not match.

faults.quote: The biggest change is how the piece is built as speech: the proposal leads, then the problem on the ground...
faults.why: The lesson claims a restructuring that did not occur, since the order is the writer's own. It is generic, and the takeaway is mostly 'add Here's the thing'.

judge.verdict: A faithful but thin rewrite: facts are intact, but it is mostly the draft with Obama tags, including an odd 'walks' and a spurious 'that's why' close. The notes and lesson overclaim a restructuring that didn't happen and teach little.
