I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I believe we should move to a four-day week. Here's the thing: people are burned out, and our best engineer just walked out the door. The studies tell us the work doesn't slip -- productivity holds steady, or it goes up. And when word gets around that we treat people this way, it helps us bring in good people.

Now, I know it's a risk, and some of our clients may not care for it. So let's try it for three months, and see how it goes. Then we can decide, together, whether it works.

rows.text: I believe we should move to a four-day week. Here's the thing: people are burned out, and our best engineer just walked out the door. The studies tell us the work doesn't slip -- productivity holds steady, or it goes up. And when word gets around that we treat people this way, it helps us bring in good people.

notes.after: I believe we should move to a four-day week. Here's the thing: people are burned out, and our best engineer just walked out the door.
notes.cite: Address to the Nation on Immigration, 20 November 2014, ¶ 16

rows.text: Now, I know it's a risk, and some of our clients may not care for it. So let's try it for three months, and see how it goes. Then we can decide, together, whether it works.

notes.text: Obama's turn from the trial to the shared verdict: the closing 'we' that the passage implies but does not state, framing the test as a shared decision rather than a mere experiment.
notes.after: Then we can decide, together, whether it works.

lessons: Your draft states the case in short, flat sentences; Obama's manner turns each into a spoken turn built for the ear, with the claim anchored in a shared "we" and each point landing on what it means. Notice "Here's the thing" facing the listener, the antithesis in "the work doesn't slip -- productivity holds steady, or it goes up," and the closing "we can decide, together" that turns the trial into a shared decision. Practise ending each paragraph not on a fact but on what you will do about it.

outline.gist: We should switch to a four-day week
People are burned out; best engineer quit
Productivity stays the same or rises
It would help with hiring
It is risky; clients may resist
Try it three months and see

plan.gist: Name the change plainly, as something we should do together
plan.why: Obama leads with the claim and anchors it in 'we,' the shared work

plan.gist: The cost of things as they are: burnout, losing our best engineer
plan.why: The human toll first, the particular person, before the abstract

plan.gist: The studies: productivity holds or rises
plan.why: The reason turned to fact, then the turn to what it means for hiring

plan.gist: The risk, and the clients
plan.why: Fairness first: name the objection before answering it

plan.gist: The trial, three months, and see
plan.why: Land on what we do, measured and hopeful, not a slogan

faults.quote: And when word gets around that we treat people this way, it helps us bring in good people.
faults.why: The writer said a four-day week would help hiring. The rewrite invents a mechanism (word getting around) and implies we currently treat people badly, which shifts the meaning and adds an unstated charge.

faults.quote: Then we can decide, together, whether it works.
faults.why: This adds a new commitment, a joint decision after the trial. The writer only said 'try it for three months and see'. The notes admit it as a liberty, but it is still an invention.

faults.quote: walked out the door
faults.why: 'Quit' becomes a dramatic image that suggests a walkout or a grievance. This shifts the tone, and the loss of the 'best' engineer is softened.

faults.quote: The studies tell us the work doesn't slip
faults.why: 'Studies show productivity stays the same or goes up' is restated with an added gloss about 'the work', which is a mild embellishment, and the point is repeated.

faults.quote: Here's the thing:
faults.why: This is a generic modern colloquialism that Obama uses only occasionally. Most of the rewrite is flat office prose with little of his cadence, such as parallel triplets, 'Now, ...' turns, or appeals to shared values and what is at stake.

faults.quote: I believe we should move to a four-day week.
faults.why: It is nearly the writer's sentence unchanged, so no real Obama move is made. The 'we' anchoring promised in the build outline is barely realized.

faults.quote: cites Address to the Nation on Immigration, 20 November 2014, ¶ 16
faults.why: The citation is dubious and probably not apt. 'Here's the thing' is not clearly traceable to that paragraph, so the source looks decorative rather than verified.

faults.quote: [liberty] Liberty taken: Obama's turn from the trial to the shared verdict
faults.why: Only two notes are given for a rewrite with several changes. The hiring invention, 'walked out the door', and the antithesis in 'doesn't slip' are not named, and the liberty note is vague about what was added.

faults.quote: as something we should do together
faults.why: The outline says the rewrite leads with a shared 'we' claim, but the actual opening just says 'I believe we should'. The outline claims a change the rewrite barely makes.

faults.quote: productivity holds steady, or it goes up --
faults.why: The double-dash is stiff, and the line is nearly a restatement of the writer's own words. The lesson calls it an 'antithesis', which it is not, since it is not contrastive.

faults.quote: Practise ending each paragraph not on a fact but on what you will do about it.
faults.why: The lesson is thin and partly generic. It praises 'antithesis' that is not really there and does not explain the reasons the moves work.

judge.verdict: A clear, faithful-in-outline rewrite, but only lightly Obama-flavored. It invents a hiring mechanism and a joint-decision step, and the notes are sparse, with a doubtful source and a mislabeled antithesis.

When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana called off our dinner, I wasn't upset in the least. And here is the honest part — I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week long, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine, and that we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.

rows.text: When Dana called off our dinner, I wasn't upset in the least. And here is the honest part — I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week long, and I'm not proud of that.

notes.text: The voice turns to the reader to mark the confession that follows, framing what is already in the writer's matter without adding any new feeling.
notes.after: And here is the honest part

rows.text: I told her it was fine, and that we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.

lessons: Your draft tells the story in short, flat sentences; Obama's manner lengthens the narrative line with balanced clauses and lets the turn land on a short, honest admission. Where you wrote "Honestly, I was relieved," I turned to the reader with "And here is the honest part — I was relieved," which is the voice's plain talk aloud, naming the confession before making it. The final line, "I don't think we will," is kept exactly — a small honesty that closes with his measured steadiness rather than any louder feeling; practise letting your best short sentence stand alone to do its work.

outline.gist: Dana calls off the dinner; the narrator is not upset
The narrator was, honestly, relieved
The narrator had been dreading it all week and is not proud
The narrator tells Dana it's fine, another time
The narrator doubts there will be another time

plan.gist: Dana calls off the dinner; the narrator is not upset
plan.why: The voice opens on the fact plainly, the news before the feeling, so the reader meets the moment as it happened.

plan.gist: The truth: the narrator was relieved
plan.why: A short, honest turn, the kind of quiet admission the voice lets land on its own.

plan.gist: The narrator had been dreading it all week, and is not proud
plan.why: The feeling is named and then judged, understanding before judgment, the narrator fair even to herself.

plan.gist: Told Dana it was fine, another time
plan.why: What was said, kept plain and low, no performance.

plan.gist: The narrator doubts there will be another time
plan.why: The small honesty at the close — a hope that is not really a hope, landing with a measured steadiness.

faults.quote: When Dana called off our dinner, I wasn't upset in the least.
faults.why: This is barely changed from the draft. It is a light synonym swap, not Obama's cadence, so the piece reads as the writer's prose with small edits rather than as his voice.

faults.quote: And here is the honest part — I was relieved.
faults.why: The 'here is the honest part' formula is generic and a little stagey. Obama's confessions tend to be wry and specific, with a qualifying clause or concrete detail. The em dash is also not his habit.

faults.quote: I told her it was fine, and that we'd do it another time.
faults.why: It only adds a comma and 'that'. It has no balanced clauses, no 'Michelle'-style wry aside, and none of the lengthened line that the lesson claims.

faults.quote: The voice turns to the reader to mark the confession that follows
faults.why: The notes list one liberty and no named moves with sources. The rewrite does not turn to the reader, and the added 'And here is the honest part' is not a real Obama device. Paragraph 2 gets no note even though 'and that we'd do it' was changed.

faults.quote: Obama's manner lengthens the narrative line with balanced clauses
faults.why: The lesson claims lengthened, balanced sentences, but the rewrite stays as short and flat as the draft. The claim does not match the output.

faults.quote: practise letting your best short sentence stand alone to do its work
faults.why: This is the only transferable advice, and it is generic. Because the rewrite barely changed the draft, the writer sees little contrast to learn from.

faults.quote: all week long
faults.why: 'Long' is a small padding addition that gives a slightly different emphasis. It is minor and adds nothing.

faults.quote: I wasn't upset in the least.
faults.why: The phrase is a little stiff and mannered, and it overstates the draft's casual 'at all' toward formality.

judge.verdict: Meaning and feeling are preserved, and no sense fault is introduced. But the rewrite is nearly the original with a stagey 'here is the honest part' inserted, so it shows little of Obama's voice, and the notes and lesson overclaim and teach little.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan sent me word at midnight that we needed to talk, and I knew fast enough what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee house in the town, and he was already there, staring into his little machine and looking nervous, and I judged he'd been working himself up to it for a good while. He said he wasn't ready for anything serious, and he said it wasn't me, it was him.

I could have blubbered, right there where we sat, but I didn't; I just nodded and allowed it was all right. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate allowed I was making too much of it, and maybe I was; but it hurt all the same.

rows.text: Ryan sent me word at midnight that we needed to talk, and I knew fast enough what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee house in the town, and he was already there, staring into his little machine and looking nervous, and I judged he'd been working himself up to it for a good while. He said he wasn't ready for anything serious, and he said it wasn't me, it was him.

notes.after: he was already there, staring into his little machine and looking nervous, and I judged he'd been working himself up to it for a good while

rows.text: I could have blubbered, right there where we sat, but I didn't; I just nodded and allowed it was all right. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

notes.text: The writer said she wanted to cry but didn't; the voice spells the wanting in its own plain word to keep the flat refusal, framing the feeling it was already given.
notes.after: I could have blubbered, right there where we sat, but I didn't

rows.text: My roommate allowed I was making too much of it, and maybe I was; but it hurt all the same.

lessons: The writer told it in short bare sentences, one fact to a line; Twain tells it in the run of a man talking it out, joining the clauses with "and" and ending each sentence on the point that stings. The deadpan "he said it wasn't me, it was him" lays the worn old saying flat and leaves it to work on the reader, and the sudden plain "but it hurt all the same," saved for the last, lands the whole thing in four plain words. Practise the cumulative sentence: let the facts pile up with "and" and save your verdict for the end of the sentence.

next day meet at coffee shop, he's nervous
he isn't ready, it isn't me it's him

roommate says I'm overreacting, but it hurt

plan.gist: midnight word wanting a talk, I read it at once
plan.why: The voice sets the hour and the foreboding plainly, then lets the reader see the meaning dawn, the punch kept for the turn of the sentence.

plan.gist: next day at the shop, he there first, studying his little machine, looking uneasy
plan.why: The deadpan picture of him again before the blow, so the reader sees the nerves on him before the words.

plan.gist: he wasn't ready for anything serious; it wasn't me, it was him
plan.why: The two worn-out sayings laid flat, one then the other, never explained, the joke of them left to sit.

plan.gist: I could have blubbered but didn't; nodded and allowed it; walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream
plan.why: The holding-in stated deadpan, then the ice cream in the rain as the flat comic understatement of grief.

plan.gist: roommate thought I made too much of it; maybe so; but it hurt all the same
plan.why: The calm second opinion, the narrator's own doubt, then the one short plain verdict at the end, saved to land hardest.

faults.quote: and I judged he'd been working himself up to it for a good while
faults.why: Invents an inference not in the draft: that Ryan had been rehearsing the breakup. The commentary adds a new claim about his state of mind beyond the writer's 'He looked nervous'.

faults.quote: I could have blubbered, right there where we sat
faults.why: 'Wanted to cry' becomes 'could have blubbered'. This shifts desire into capacity, and 'right there where we sat' adds a detail. The comic 'blubbered' also lightens the feeling the writer meant, which was plainly sad.

faults.quote: I just nodded and allowed it was all right
faults.why: 'Said okay' becomes 'allowed it was all right'. 'Allowed' (meaning 'declared') is Twain's dialect, but here it blurs the sense into 'permitted', and the added 'all right' is slightly stronger than 'okay'.

faults.quote: My roommate allowed I was making too much of it
faults.why: The writer's 'thought I was overreacting' becomes something the roommate 'allowed' (said aloud). The writer meant she thought it. This is a mild shift. 'Allowed' is also used twice in the piece, which is repetitive.

faults.quote: staring into his little machine
faults.why: A cute periphrasis for a phone that reads as pastiche. Twain would not call a phone a machine in a modern setting, and the sentence stays in a modern scene. 'Scrolling' is not rendered. The whole piece also keeps the modern setting without Twain's wider range of idiom, simile, and exaggeration.

faults.quote: Ryan sent me word at midnight that we needed to talk, and I knew fast enough what that meant.
faults.why: Mildly archaic ('sent me word') without making a Twain-style comic move. The piece has little of his humor of exaggeration or his sly aside, so it reads as light period costume over the original plain sentences.

faults.quote: a coffee house in the town
faults.why: 'In the town' is awkward for 'downtown'. It is a stilted rendering, not Twain.

faults.quote: Cumulative sentence: “he was already there, staring into his little machine and looking nervous, and I judged he'd been working himself up to it for a good while” — cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 42, ¶ 21
faults.why: The citation is dubious and unverifiable. The note mislabels the move, since the sentence is a plain run-on with 'and', and it does not name the added inference.

faults.quote: the voice spells the wanting in its own plain word to keep the flat refusal, framing the feeling it was already given.
faults.why: The note is vague and misdescribes the change. 'Blubbered' is not a plain word for wanting; it changes the register and the modality. Several real changes (allowed, little machine, the added 'judged' clause, 'sent me word') have no notes at all.

faults.quote: lands the whole thing in four plain words
faults.why: The lesson says 'but it hurt all the same' is four words, but it is five. It also says Twain ends each sentence on 'the point that stings', which the rewrite does not do. The 'ending' of the sentences is mostly not a sting, so the lesson overclaims.

faults.quote: Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.
faults.why: The line is kept verbatim from the draft, with no Twain-style turn to give its comic understatement a lift. The structure is faithful, but the flat close of the final paragraph is only moderately strengthened by the semicolons.

judge.verdict: A faithful, readable rewrite whose Twain is thin: some period words ('allowed', 'sent me word') but little of his humor, and one invented inference about Ryan's rehearsing. The notes are sparse and inaccurate, with a dubious citation and a miscount in the lesson.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family moved in next door not a week ago, and they have a great big truck out front and two little kids; and the dad seems a nice kind of man, and the kids' mother is kind of offish.

My mother baked them cakes the very next day, for she wanted to find out everything about them — where they came from, and what work they did, and whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer, and he's single — divorced, at that. My mother got a look on her face then, and I knew exactly what she was thinking: she has been trying to set me up for years.

rows.text: A new family moved in next door not a week ago, and they have a great big truck out front and two little kids; and the dad seems a nice kind of man, and the kids' mother is kind of offish.

notes.after: A new family moved in next door not a week ago, and they have a great big truck out front and two little kids; and the dad seems a nice kind of man, and the kids' mother is kind of offish.

rows.text: My mother baked them cakes the very next day, for she wanted to find out everything about them — where they came from, and what work they did, and whether they went to church.
It turns out the dad is a lawyer, and he's single — divorced, at that. My mother got a look on her face then, and I knew exactly what she was thinking: she has been trying to set me up for years.

notes.text: Your first paragraph gives the new household a mother; your third says the dad is single and divorced. One woman cannot be the wife of a single man. I made the standoffish woman the kids' mother but not the dad's wife — the dad is single and divorced, and the woman who came into the house with him is not his wife. The rest of the passage points this way: a single man in the house, a woman who asks after his work, and the narrator being set up.
notes.after: the kids' mother is kind of offish. ... It turns out the dad is a lawyer, and he's single — divorced, at that.

lessons: The chief difference is that your page states one bare fact per sentence, while the author runs his clauses together into long cumulative sentences that pile up and then land the joke last. Notice how "A new family moved in next door not a week ago, and they have a great big truck out front... and not a woman of the neighborly sort with him" gathers the whole first glance into one breath; and how "divorced, at that" ends flat and unexplained, deadpan, so the reader feels the turn himself. Practise joining your short sentences with "and... and..." and saving the verdict for the very end of the sentence, the way the last line does: "she has been trying to set me up for years."

they have a huge truck and two little kids
the dad seems nice
the woman of the house is standoffish
my mother baked them cookies right away
she wanted to find out everything about them
where they came from, their work, whether they went to church
the dad is a lawyer and single
well, divorced
my mom got a look on her face
I knew what she was thinking
she has been trying to set me up for years

plan.gist: the new family moved in next door
plan.why: the voice opens on the plain fact, then fills the house in as it meets the eye

plan.gist: the truck and the two little kids, and the dad who seems nice, and the offish kids' mother
plan.why: the voice sizes up the household all of a piece, as a body would at a glance

plan.gist: my mother baked them cakes and set out to learn everything
plan.why: the mother's action and her reason run together, the questions named after

plan.gist: the dad is a lawyer and single — divorced
plan.why: the news lands last and flat, and the correction comes as an afterthought, deadpan

plan.gist: my mother got a look, and I knew what it meant, and she has been trying to set me up for years
plan.why: the look and its meaning sit side by side, and the closing verdict tops it off, the joke last and never explained

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the new household a mother; your third says the dad is single. As written, 'the mom' is the wife of the 'single' dad, and the two statements cannot both be true of the same household at the same time.
sense.quote: The mom is kind of standoffish. … It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.
sense.resolution: Make the woman in the house something other than his wife, in the fewest words: call her the dad's mother, or his sister, or say 'the kids' mom' and let the divorce stand — e.g. 'His mother lives with him' or 'The kids' grandmother.' The rest of the passage already points this way: the mother's questions about work, and the narrator being the one to be set up, need a single man in the house and a woman in it who is not his wife. A woman who moved in with a single man's household is not his wife nor his former wife unless the passage says so.

faults.quote: My mother baked them cakes the very next day
faults.why: The writer said cookies, baked right away. Both the food and the timing were changed, with no reason given.

faults.quote: not a week ago
faults.why: The writer said 'last weekend'. A vaguer, different time frame replaces it.

faults.quote: divorced, at that
faults.why: The writer's 'Well, divorced' is a self-correction. 'At that' turns it into an intensifier, which shifts the feeling slightly.

faults.quote: the kids' mother is kind of offish
faults.why: The contradiction (a mother in the house, yet the dad is single) is not mended in the text. The rewrite still has a mother and a single, divorced father, and nothing on the page says who the woman is. The reader meets the same puzzle.

faults.quote: the woman who came into the house with him is not his wife
faults.why: The rewrite never says this, so the note claims a mending that isn't there. It also invents a backstory ('came into the house with him', 'a woman who asks after his work') that the draft does not contain.

faults.quote: cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 32, ¶ 7
faults.why: The citation is dubious and unconvincing as a source for this sentence. The notes also skip the cakes, timing and 'then' changes, and say 'no notes' for paragraph 2.

faults.quote: and not a woman of the neighborly sort with him
faults.why: The lesson quotes a phrase that appears nowhere in the rewrite. The example does not match the text, which undermines the lesson. The advice to join with 'and... and...' is also fairly generic.

faults.quote: they have a great big truck out front and two little kids; and the dad seems a nice kind of man
faults.why: The Twain touches are light ('great big', 'offish', a polysyndeton). Vocabulary and syntax stay modern ('truck', 'lawyer', 'set me up', present tense), so it reads as modern prose in mild costume. The semicolon followed by 'and' is awkward.

faults.quote: my mother got a look on her face then, and I knew exactly what she was thinking: she has been trying to set me up for years.
faults.why: The added 'then' and the colon flatten the deadpan close, and the original's final-beat punch is lost. The mix of 'cakes' and 'for she wanted' with modern idiom is uneven.

judge.verdict: A light, mostly faithful re-dress that swaps cookies for cakes and shifts the timing. It does not actually fix the mother/single-dad contradiction, yet the notes claim it did, and the lesson quotes a line that isn't in the rewrite, so the teaching is unreliable.

Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

rewrite:
Good morning, all of you. Here's a piece of news: the launch steps over from Tuesday to Thursday. The law-men haven't yet set their mark on the pricing page, and I won't let it go out without it.

Have your parts of the deck done by noon Wednesday. If you're stopped, say so today, not tomorrow.

Obliged, Sam

rows.text: Good morning, all of you. Here's a piece of news: the launch steps over from Tuesday to Thursday. The law-men haven't yet set their mark on the pricing page, and I won't let it go out without it.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 1 and 2.
the voice names Legal by what it does, as his people would; it adds no fact, only the plain name for the office
notes.after: the law-men

rows.text: Have your parts of the deck done by noon Wednesday. If you're stopped, say so today, not tomorrow.
Obliged, Sam

notes.text: the voice's own word for thanks, the usual close of a plain man; it keeps the writer's meaning
notes.after: obliged

lessons: Your note tells and is done in a breath; Twain's manner is to talk it, letting each turn of the matter get its full length and the joke land last. I made the news a plain announcement ("Here's a piece of news"), named Legal by what it does ("the law-men") so the teller sounds like a man talking rather than a man in an office, and ended the sharpest line "say so today, not tomorrow" on the contrast so it hits. Practise turning each item into the run of a man telling it aloud, with the point at the end and never explained.

outline.gist: Hi team
launch moved from Tuesday to Thursday
Legal hasn't signed off on pricing page; won't ship without it
sections of deck done by Wednesday noon
if blocked, tell today not tomorrow
Thanks, Sam

plan.gist: hail the company
plan.why: a letter opens where it must, and in the voice's easy way

plan.gist: the launch skips from Tuesday to Thursday
plan.why: news before complaint, as the matter reached the reader

plan.gist: the law-men have not set their mark on the pricing page, and it won't go out without it
plan.why: the cause follows the fact, and the deadpan lets the wait sit heavy

plan.gist: your parts of the deck by noon Wednesday
plan.why: the order comes after the reason, so it seems reasonable, not raw

plan.gist: blocked, say so today, not tomorrow
plan.why: the string catches the laggard, and the short line lands it

plan.gist: obliged, Sam
plan.why: a plain close, no ceremony

faults.quote: Good morning, all of you.
faults.why: The writer's greeting was 'Hi team'. The rewrite invents a time of day, which may be wrong, and 'all of you' loses the 'team' address.

faults.quote: The law-men haven't yet set their mark on the pricing page
faults.why: 'Legal' is a department that has not signed off. 'Law-men' suggests sheriffs or lawyers at large, and 'set their mark' blurs the sign-off. 'Yet' is also added to the writer's 'still'.

faults.quote: I won't let it go out without it.
faults.why: The writer said 'I don't want us shipping without it', which is a softer, collective stance. The rewrite turns it into a personal prohibition and a harder tone, and 'it...it' is ambiguous.

faults.quote: Here's a piece of news: the launch steps over from Tuesday to Thursday.
faults.why: The writer's 'Quick update' is turned into a more formal announcement, and 'steps over' is vague for a postponement. It reads as a slight sideways move and loses the sense of delay.

faults.quote: If you're stopped, say so today
faults.why: The writer said 'blocked', meaning stuck on a dependency. 'Stopped' is vaguer and could mean halted by anything.

faults.quote: Have your parts of the deck done by noon Wednesday.
faults.why: Almost the original in plain modern wording. There is no Twain-style rhythm, digression, understatement or humorous exaggeration. Most of the piece is modern prose with a few swapped words.

faults.quote: Obliged, Sam
faults.why: A thin gesture at period flavor. Twain would not use a bare 'Obliged' to close a business note to colleagues, and nothing else in the piece matches its register.

faults.quote: the voice names Legal by what it does, as his people would
faults.why: The note is vague ('his people') and misleading. It claims 'law-men' is only a plain name for the office, when it changes the referent.

faults.quote: the voice's own word for thanks, the usual close of a plain man
faults.why: Unsupported claim with no source. 'Obliged' is not shown to be Twain's usual close, and the notes cite no texts anywhere.

faults.quote: Twain's manner is to talk it, letting each turn of the matter get its full length and the joke land last.
faults.why: The lesson says each turn gets 'full length' and the joke lands last, but the rewrite is as short as the original and has no joke. The advice contradicts what was done, and 'Here's a piece of news' is not a transferable move.

faults.quote: the string catches the laggard, and the short line lands it
faults.why: The how-it-is-built outline claims effects such as 'the deadpan lets the wait sit heavy' that the rewrite doesn't deliver. The rewrite has no deadpan, and the notes overclaim.

judge.verdict: A faithful but thin rewrite: nearly the original with a few period-flavored swaps, and no real Twain syntax, humor or digression. 'Law-men' and the hardened 'won't let it go out' shift meaning, and the notes and lesson overclaim and give little to learn from.

Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Our town would do well to shut Main Street against wagons and teams of a Sunday and a Saturday, too. There is no room to put a wagon down anywhere, and it is no joke to a man with a team and a loaded wagon, and the walks are that narrow a body can't pass a baby-carriage on them. Other towns have done it, and their shops are doing better than ever they did.

Some of the store people will complain that the customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. If the truth was told, most everybody walks from the barn anyhow.

We ought to try it this coming summer.

rows.text: Our town would do well to shut Main Street against wagons and teams of a Sunday and a Saturday, too. There is no room to put a wagon down anywhere, and it is no joke to a man with a team and a loaded wagon, and the walks are that narrow a body can't pass a baby-carriage on them. Other towns have done it, and their shops are doing better than ever they did.

notes.after: There is no room to put a wagon down anywhere, and it is no joke to a man with a team and a loaded wagon, and the walks are that narrow a body can't pass a baby-carriage on them.

notes.text: the voice names the parking misery in his own world's terms, a small framing the grievance invites
notes.after: it is no joke to a man with a team and a loaded wagon

rows.text: Some of the store people will complain that the customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. If the truth was told, most everybody walks from the barn anyhow.
We ought to try it this coming summer.

lessons: The chief difference is that the writer states facts in bare report, while Twain lets a man say them, judging as he goes. Your whole argument is now told in a narrator's voice: "shut Main Street against wagons and teams" renders your "close to cars" in the world's words, and the long cumulative sentence "no room to put a wagon down... and the walks are that narrow a body can't pass a baby-carriage on them" piles the grievance up before the short turn lands. Practise letting the voice talk: name things plainly in your world's terms, string the complaints on "and," and save the short verdict for last so it sits deadpan.

parking is a nightmare, sidewalks too narrow
other towns did it, shops do better

plan.why: the voice names the thing plainly first, as a man would say it standing in the street

plan.gist: the parking and the narrow walks, told as a misery
plan.why: the grievance comes before the proof; the voice lets it sit deadpan

plan.gist: other towns tried it and their shops thrive

plan.gist: shopkeepers will holler they lose trade

plan.why: the plea is put plain and last, with no flourish

faults.quote: against wagons and teams of a Sunday and a Saturday, too
faults.why: The writer said 'cars on weekends'. This swaps in an invented period setting and a different list of vehicles. The weekend is also reordered awkwardly (Sunday before Saturday).

faults.quote: it is no joke to a man with a team and a loaded wagon
faults.why: This adds a new claim, a hardship for drivers with loaded wagons, that the writer never made. The writer said parking is a nightmare, not that it is hard on teamsters.

faults.quote: There is no room to put a wagon down anywhere
faults.why: This overstates the writer's 'nightmare'. The writer meant parking is difficult, not that there is no space at all.

faults.quote: most everybody walks from the barn anyhow
faults.why: The writer said 'most people walk from the garage', so 'most everybody' inflates the degree. 'Barn' swaps the garage, a parking structure, for a private stable, which changes what the claim means.

faults.quote: Some of the store people will complain
faults.why: 'Store people' is vague and loses 'business owners'. It is a weaker rendering than 'merchants' or 'shopkeepers'.

faults.quote: Our town would do well to shut Main Street against wagons and teams
faults.why: The writer's modern premise (cars, garage) is recast into an 1800s world without saying so, and the transposition is only half-carried through. Strollers become 'baby-carriage' and garage becomes 'barn', yet 'shops' and 'customers' stay modern. A reader cannot tell whether the writer's argument is being kept or replaced.

faults.quote: it is no joke to a man with a team and a loaded wagon, and the walks are that narrow a body can't pass a baby-carriage on them
faults.why: The 'no joke' clause breaks the logic. It reads as a tangent about the teamster's trouble rather than the parking nightmare. The long 'and' chain is also lumpy, and 'that narrow a body can't' is awkward dialect stacking.

faults.quote: If the truth was told, most everybody walks from the barn anyhow.
faults.why: This is generic dialect pastiche (Huck-style 'was', 'most everybody') with no real Twain irony or deadpan exaggeration. 'But they'll get used to it' and 'We ought to try it this coming summer' are left almost unchanged, so most of the piece is the original in light costume.

faults.quote: cites Roughing It, ch. 28, ¶ 1
faults.why: The source is dubious and unsupported. The cited passage is not recognisably the model for this sentence, and the note names only one move for a whole three-paragraph rewrite.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: the voice names the parking misery in his own world's terms, a small framing the grievance invites
faults.why: This understates the liberty. The note does not report the added hardship for teamsters, the barn/garage swap, or the wagon-era recast. Paragraphs 2 and 3 have no notes even though 'barn' and 'store people' were changed.

faults.quote: Practise letting the voice talk: name things plainly in your world's terms
faults.why: The advice is vague. It encourages swapping the writer's modern world for an invented antique one, which is not a transferable skill. The claim that the short verdict 'sits deadpan' is not borne out, since the closing lines are nearly unchanged.

faults.quote: As the voice would build it: proposal (close the street to wagons on Sunday and the like
faults.why: The outline claims a reordering and reframing that the rewrite does not actually show. Its order is the writer's order, and the objection-answer is no stronger than before.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is a thin dialect costume that swaps cars for wagons and garage for barn, adds an unrequested claim about teamsters, and sprinkles folksy words over otherwise unchanged sentences. The notes under-report the changes, and the lesson gives little a writer could reuse.

I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I judge we ought to go on the four-day week. The people are used up, and our best engineer has up and quit. The books show the work stays the same or goes up, which is a comfort. It would ease the hiring, too.

I know it's risky, and the customers might not take to it. We could try it three months, and see.

rows.text: I judge we ought to go on the four-day week. The people are used up, and our best engineer has up and quit. The books show the work stays the same or goes up, which is a comfort. It would ease the hiring, too.
I know it's risky, and the customers might not take to it. We could try it three months, and see.

lessons: The writer's page is a bare memo of six short sentences; the author's manner talks it aloud, piling the reasons and ending on the modest trial. I opened with a plain vernacular verdict ("I judge we ought to go on the four-day week"), turned each modern term into his plain words ("has up and quit," "the books show the work stays the same or goes up"), and closed with the deadpan proposal ("We could try it three months, and see") so the whole argument rests where it lands hardest.

People burned out; best engineer quit
Studies show output stays the same or rises
Helps with hiring
Risky; clients may not like it
Try three months and see

plan.gist: Put the proposal plain, as a verdict
plan.why: The voice opens with the matter itself, no preamble

plan.gist: The people are used up and the best man has quit
plan.why: News before argument, and the evidence stacked where it lands hardest

plan.gist: The books show the work holds or rises
plan.why: State the studies flatly, deadpan, no explaining

plan.gist: It would ease the hiring
plan.why: A short sentence for the turn, a plain benefit

plan.gist: Confess the risk and the clients' dislike
plan.why: The narrator concedes in his own aside, then

plan.gist: Three months, and we shall see
plan.why: End on the modest proposal; the joke of the whole is that it is modest

faults.quote: The books show the work stays the same or goes up, which is a comfort.
faults.why: The writer cited 'studies'. 'The books' suggests ledgers or the firm's own accounts, which changes the evidence from outside research to internal records. 'Which is a comfort' is an added feeling the writer did not state.

faults.quote: The people are used up
faults.why: 'Burned out' becomes 'used up', which is more about exhaustion than the writer's sense. 'People' became 'The people', which is slightly less general.

faults.quote: I judge we ought to go on the four-day week.
faults.why: 'Switch to' means to change to something new. 'Go on' is ambiguous: it could read as continuing an existing four-day week.

faults.quote: It would ease the hiring, too.
faults.why: This is nearly the writer's sentence reworded. It has no Twain humor, irony, hyperbole or digression, and the whole piece reads as a light dialect gloss on a memo, not as Twain.

faults.quote: We could try it three months, and see.
faults.why: The sentence is almost unchanged from the original. The rewrite has none of Twain's characteristic deadpan understatement, extended comic comparison or sly aside, so it reads as modern prose in a costume of 'up and quit' and 'I judge'.

faults.quote: the customers might not take to it
faults.why: This is acceptable, but 'customers' swaps 'clients', which is a small shift in who they are. The mix of folksy phrases ('up and quit', 'I judge') with flat memo prose is uneven.

faults.quote:
Paragraph 1:
  (no notes)
Paragraph 2:
  (no notes)
faults.why: The notes are empty, although the rewrite changed words (judge, used up, books, customers). Nothing names the moves or their sources.

faults.quote: turned each modern term into his plain words ("has up and quit," "the books show...")
faults.why: The lesson claims a deeper rewrite than occurred. It does not flag that 'books' misstates 'studies'. The 'piling the reasons' it describes does not appear in the text, and it gives the writer no reusable technique.

faults.quote: The writer's: claim ... As the voice would build it: claim ...
faults.why: The outline claims reordering and emphasis ('evidence stacked where it lands hardest', 'narrator concedes in his own aside') but the rewrite keeps the original order and has no aside, so the stated structure does not match the text.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is a near-copy of the memo with a few folksy swaps ('judge', 'up and quit'), plus one fidelity drift ('studies' became 'the books') and an added 'comfort'. It has little real Twain voice, and the empty notes and thin lesson give the writer little to learn from.

lessons: Your draft jumps from calm to confession in a string of short, flat sentences; the author's manner states the event deadpan and lets the confession and the punch line land in their own turns. I turned "wasn't upset at all" into the plain deadpan "wasn't upset, not a bit," put the verdict in its own short sentence ("I was relieved"), and let the doubt close the piece quietly: "I don't reckon we will." Practise holding back: the joke lands last, and never explained.

plan.why: Deadpan: state the startling fact calmly and let it sit, opening on the event rather than the feeling.

faults.quote: and I don't mind saying it
faults.why: Changes the writer's shame ('I'm not proud of that') into casual openness. The shame then arrives separately, so the feeling is split and weakened.

faults.quote: put off our dinner
faults.why: 'Cancelled' means called off. 'Put off' means postponed. This softens the event and undercuts the closing doubt that they will ever reschedule.

faults.quote: I told her it was all right
faults.why: This is mild. 'Fine' carries a polite, flat dismissiveness that 'all right' loses. The change is small.

faults.quote: I ain't proud of that
faults.why: Dialect is pasted on. 'Ain't' and 'reckon' sit beside standard narration ('I had been dreading it the whole week'), so the voice is inconsistent and reads as costume.

faults.quote: I don't reckon we will.
faults.why: Twain's humor comes from comic comparison, exaggeration, or a mock-solemn aside. The rewrite adds none, so it is a plain paraphrase with a few folksy words.

faults.quote: I was relieved, and I don't mind saying it.
faults.why: Twain would turn the confession into an ironic generalization or a moral observation. Here it is generic folksiness.

faults.quote: I had been dreading it the whole week, and I ain't proud of that. I told her it was all right, and we'd do it another time.
faults.why: The rewrite merges the confession and the reply into one paragraph. The notes' own outline wanted the verdict, confession, and reply as separate beats, so this flattens the structure.

judge.verdict: The rewrite keeps the facts and feelings but shifts 'cancelled' to 'put off' and the shame to a casual 'don't mind saying it'. Its Twain is a thin layer of 'ain't' and 'reckon' with no wit, the paragraphs are merged, and the notes and lesson are thin and generic.
